summary: Lists functional requirements for using the Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture with GMPLS networks. The PCE work had first focused on MPLS, and this is the follow-on for the wider set of switching technologies GMPLS covers.

eli5.summary: A trip planner first learned roads only. This lists what it must learn to plan trips over trains and ships too.

subtitle: What the Path Computation Element framework must add to serve GMPLS networks such as WDM, TDM and Ethernet.

tldr.problem: The PCE work first focused on MPLS, but GMPLS-controlled networks (such as WDM, TDM or Ethernet) have extra constraints that a path computation request and reply must be able to carry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 13 attributes a path computation request should be able to express and three additions a reply needs: handling of concatenation, label constraints, and the roles of working and protection routes.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only: it asks for extensions to PCE-related protocols and does not define the protocol changes itself.

sections.title: Why GMPLS Needs More from PCE
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) working group first concentrated on path computation inside a domain, or across domains, in MPLS networks. Service providers also want path computation for GMPLS-controlled networks, such as those based on Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM), Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) or Ethernet.

RFC 4655 and RFC 4657 already discuss the framework and requirements for PCE on both packet MPLS and GMPLS networks. This document complements them with considerations for intradomain and interdomain GMPLS, and lists requirements for extending the PCE-related protocols. Interlayer and inter-area traffic engineering, covered in RFC 6457 and RFC 4927, is out of scope.

Computing a path for a GMPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) is usually more demanding than for an MPLS TE LSP because more constraints apply: interface switching capability, link encoding, link protection capability and Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG).
sections.eli5: Planning a route for a car is simple. Planning one for a train that also needs the right kind of track and the right kind of wagons has more rules, and the planner must know them.

sections.title: GMPLS Applications of PCE
sections.content:
The RFC uses a four-node model with an ingress link, a transit link and an egress link. It assumes the switching capabilities of the outgoing links from the ingress and egress nodes agree, that all transit links match the switching type of the LSP to be created, and that their encoding types match the LSP's encoding type.

As an example it takes a Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) network. A client Ethernet service of 100 Mbit/s from A1 to A2 could ride in one Virtual Container 4 (VC-4) or in three concatenated VC-3s. The Path Computation Client (PCC), such as the ingress node or a Network Management System, may choose the container type, or the PCE may decide it based on policy. If the PCC chooses, it should state the ingress and egress nodes, signal type, type of concatenation and number of concatenation in its PCReq message.

Two further needs are named. Unnumbered interface IDs (RFC 3477) must be indicatable in the PCReq, including paths that mix numbered and unnumbered links. And since RFC 6387 allows asymmetric bandwidth bidirectional LSPs, the PCC should be able to ask for different bandwidth in the forward and reverse directions.
sections.eli5: Say you want to send a big parcel. You could use one large truck or three small ones. The planner needs to be told which you want, or choose on its own, and then find roads that fit.

sections.title: Requirements on the Path Computation Request
sections.content:
A request from a PCC or another PCE must carry enough information for the PCE to consider the GMPLS TE attributes. The RFC lists 13, including:

  • Switching capability or type, and encoding type, with all current and future values.
  • Signal type, concatenation type and concatenation number.
  • Technology-specific labels.
  • End-to-end path protection type, such as 1+1 protection, 1:1 protection or pre-planned rerouting.
  • Administrative group and link protection type.
  • Support for unnumbered interfaces and for asymmetric bandwidth requests.
  • Explicit label control, and label restrictions similar to the RSVP-TE ERO and XRO.

Concatenation comes in two kinds. Contiguous concatenation requires co-routing of each member signal and support on all interfaces along the path. Virtual concatenation allows diverse routing of member signals and needs support only at the ingress and egress interfaces.
sections.eli5: When you ask the planner for a route you must tell it all the details: what kind of vehicle, how big, and any special needs. The list of details is longer for these special networks.

sections.title: Requirements on the Path Computation Reply
sections.content:
The PCEP PCRep message must be extended to meet three requirements.

  • Concatenation. For contiguous concatenation, a single route is required and only one ERO should carry it. For virtual concatenation there may be diverse routes, so multiple EROs may be needed. When one ERO stands for several member signals, the number must be specified.
  • Label constraint. If the PCC did not give exact labels and the PCE can do route and label assignment, the PCE needs to be able to put the label of the path in the PCRep. Wavelength restriction is a typical case.
  • Roles of the routes. When the PCC specifies a protection type, the PCE should compute the working route and the protection routes. The PCRep should allow them to be told apart, so RSVP-TE can create both LSPs, for example with the ASSOCIATION object (RFC 6689).
sections.eli5: The planner's answer has to say more too: one route or several, which lanes to use, and which route is the main one and which is the backup.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
The RFC changes no management or operational details for PCE networks. It does propose new PCEP objects and data, so these elements will need to appear in management tools and in the PCE MIB modules that model PCEP deployments.

On security, PCEP extensions for GMPLS fall under the same security as current PCE work and do not change the underlying issues. Section 10 of RFC 5440 lists PCEP security considerations. Since the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO, RFC 5925) has now been published, PCEP implementations should fully support it according to RFC 6952.
sections.eli5: The new features are guarded the same way the old ones are, and the connection should use the newer lock called TCP-AO.

messages.label: PCReq
messages.note: Carries the GMPLS attributes such as signal type, concatenation and protection type.

messages.label: PCRep
messages.note: Carries the computed route(s), labels, and the working or protection role of each.
